claim: An insertion effect's output level byte is a multiplier stored as a whole number over a hundred and twenty-seven, and that multiplier is not the byte. Every one of the hundred and twenty-five settings the run could read returns a gain that sits on the 1/127 grid: a median 0.0225 of a step away, against 0.2185 for the next best denominator of the sixty-one asked and 0.25 for a number that sat on no grid at all. What the entries are is a curve and not a formula -- the multiplier is three quarters of the byte over the bottom quarter of the range and rises to the byte itself at the top, and no law in the catalogue crosses that. The byte read straight as the multiplier is out by a median 1.61 decibels and by 3.53 at setting 9.
named: a stored table of seven-bit multipliers, one per setting

measurements.read_as: The level of the whole take at every setting of the byte, and the spread the run's own repeats of one setting drew. The band profiles in the same record are not used here: a level byte scales what reaches it, so the figure that answers this class is the one that does not know how the bands were cut. The same takes are also published at a twelfth of an octave and carry the identical levels, so scoring both would count one measurement twice.

The bypass control, which is why this claim says nothing about the absolute gain. Routed past the effect the take is 0.30 dB louder than with the effect in at its loudest setting -- but the same control differs from the flat setting by up to 0.37 dB band by band, so the chain is not transparent when its gains are centred and the 0.30 cannot be attributed to the level byte. The byte over 127 and the byte over 128 differ by 0.068 dB and are the same law under this record.

measurements.why: The same address on a type built round a modulator and a delay line rather than round four filter sections, with the modulator's depth parked and the balance fully across to the effect. Fifteen settings weighted towards the bottom of the byte, which is the only stretch where the stored curve and the laws part company by more than the reading resolves.

The same address on a type whose output stops being proportional to its input, with the amp simulator switched out so the drive is the type's own nonlinearity and nothing else, and the drive at three quarters. The type prints no balance, so none of the signal goes past the row being read.

The same sweep on the same type with the drive at nothing. Held against the one above it says whether the byte is applied after the saturating stage or inside it, which a single sweep of any type cannot say. It is also the reading in this class that stands furthest over its own floor, so it reaches further down the byte than either type before it.

document_rows.read_as: Evidence that a page prints that range against that address, and nothing about the unit. What the claim takes from it is that the byte has a hundred and twenty-eight settings and no printed quantity beside them -- the page names no decibels, so there is nothing here to hold a measured gain against and the whole of what the multiplier is comes from the sweep.

community.claim: In the same reverse-engineering record this archive already cites for the frequency class, a gain parameter of that rendering indexes a stored table rather than being used as a multiplier, and a byte past the table's end is ignored rather than clamped. That is the same shape as the claim here and it is not the same parameter: what was read there is an equaliser's gain in decibels, printed -12 - +12 and holding a handful of entries, while this is an effect's output level, printed 0 - 127. So it carries the claim no further than the era prior above already does -- that a maker of this line stored gains rather than computing them -- and it says nothing about the denominator, about a table this long, or about what the entries are. The two were read in the same session and this claim was made from the sweep first.
community.source: The TabulaSonora project's reverse-engineering record of the Roland SOUND Canvas VA voice: docs/FINDINGS.md in its spec repository, and the insertion-effect source of its NativeTS engine. Read 2026-09-13.

era_priors.claim: A gain is one number, so a table of a hundred and twenty-eight of them costs a hundred and twenty-eight bytes and nothing about the period argues for a runtime formula instead.
era_priors.why: This is the opposite of what the same period implies about a frequency parameter, and the difference is what is stored per entry. A filter entry is a set of coefficients, so entries are expensive and the table is short -- sixteen of them, which is the finding on 40 03 07. A gain entry is one multiplier, so the table can be as long as the byte and the designer is free to put any curve in it.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: The measured multipliers followed a law cheap enough to evaluate at speed, which would say the table was not written even though it could have been. Four such laws were held against the sweep and the best is out by a median 1.61 decibels.

era_priors.claim: A denominator of a hundred and twenty-seven says the numbers were stored rather than computed.
era_priors.why: Dividing by 127 is not arithmetic a fixed-point part of this period does per sample; dividing by 128 is a shift. A table written so that the top of the byte reaches exactly unity has 127 as its denominator for free, because the table is the division. So the denominator is not only a quantum, it is a statement about where the arithmetic happened.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: The grid had turned out to be 128 or a power of two, which the scan asked and which sits with every other losing denominator at a fifth of a step away.

adds: The record says how loud the take was at each of the hundred and twenty-eight settings, and says in as many words that no law, no curve and no quantum is in it. Nothing in it says the gains land on a grid, which grid, that the grid means the numbers were stored, or that the byte is not the multiplier. That is the whole of what is added, and it is added by scanning every nearby denominator and by holding four candidate laws against the same readings.

the_quantum.how_it_was_read: Every admitted setting's multiplier against the loudest, times a candidate denominator, and how far the results sit from whole numbers. The scan over sixty-one denominators is the control: one denominator tried alone returns a small number with nothing to read it against, which is a negative with no stated sensitivity.

settings_left_out.why: 1.1 dB above the same chain's silence, and a level is not read below 20
15.3 dB above the same chain's silence, and a level is not read below 20
15.3 dB above the same chain's silence, and a level is not read below 20

the_quantum.and_not_a_finer_grid: At a denominator of 254 every one of the hundred and twenty-five entries comes back even, so the finer grid is the same grid counted twice and the quantum is 1/127. At 381, which is three times 127, sixty-four come back odd, which is what a multiple of the real quantum does.
the_quantum.what_it_does_not_say: Nothing about the curve. A grid this fine has a point near any number, so the values of the table are not evidence for the grid and the grid is not evidence for the values. The scan reads how far the unrounded measurements sit from the grid, which is the only part of this that a table of a hundred and twenty-five free integers cannot arrange to be small.

the_table.read_as: The multipliers the sweep returned, rounded to whole numbers over 127. A readout and not a law: it is the measurement in the units the quantum gives it, published because that is the form anything downstream needs, and it is kept out of the candidate ranking for the same reason. Rounding every measured multiplier onto the grid costs a median 0.0059 dB and at worst 0.0355, against a floor of 0.1655 -- which says the rounding loses nothing, not that the grid is right. The scan says that.
the_table.why: Setting 0, whose take sits 1.1 decibels above what the same chain recorded with nothing played on every record that asked it. A level read that close to the floor is the room's. It is filled with the straight line the byte gives and named rather than left as a hole.
the_table.the_shape_of_it: Monotone, 127 at the top, and eleven settings where it does not move beside eleven where it moves by two. Three quarters of the byte from setting 4 to setting 32, to the entry -- 3, 6, 12 and 24 -- and then a ratio that climbs to one at the top. Six decibels per doubling of the byte over the bottom three octaves of it, which is what a multiplier proportional to the byte does, at three quarters the size.

held_out.what: The same entries, read off the first type's sweep, held against the second type's. On the record they were read from they are the measurement agreeing with itself and mean nothing. On this one they were not fitted to anything: eleven settings, a type they have never seen.
held_out.read_as: A median 0.011 dB and a worst 0.042, against a floor of 0.166 -- under the floor at every setting, and not leaning. That is a prediction and not a fit, and it is the only figure in this file the readout has earned. It is still not in the ranking: what it would be ranked against is the record it was made from.

two_entries_that_were_not_readings.what_changed: Settings 1 and 2 were placeholders and are readings. On the first type they stood 15.3 dB over the same chain's silence, which is under this class's own rule of twenty, and they were filled with the straight line the byte gives -- 1 and 2. The third type's driven sweep stands far enough above the same floor to read them: 1 at 22.4 dB over the silence, 2 at 22.4 dB over the silence.
two_entries_that_were_not_readings.what_it_costs_the_readout: Those two settings are the measurement agreeing with itself on the record that supplied them, so they are left out of every figure scored against it -- and the entry that moved is why the figure matters. Scored with them in, the readout carrying the old placeholder is out by 6.0 dB at setting 2 against a floor of 0.166, which is the placeholder being wrong and not the reading being poor.
two_entries_that_were_not_readings.why_one_moved_and_one_did_not: The straight line put 1 at setting 1 and 2 at setting 2, and the readings put 1 at both. So the fill was right once by arithmetic and wrong once, which is what a fill is -- and the table now has a pair of settings returning one multiplier at the bottom, where before it had a step. Eleven other settings of the hundred and twenty-eight return the multiplier of the setting before them, so a repeat there is the shape the rest of the table already has rather than a new thing to explain.
two_entries_that_were_not_readings.not_folded_into_the_quantum: The denominator scan is the first record's, over the hundred and twenty-five settings it admitted, and it is not re-run here. Two entries added to a hundred and twenty-five would not move a winner that stands at 0.0225 of a step against a runner-up at 0.2185, and a scan re-run to fold in the two settings that moved would be a scan re-run after seeing which way they went.

alternatives.reading: The multiplier is the byte over 128 rather than over 127, which is the divide the part can actually do.
alternatives.why_not_separable: The two differ by a constant 0.068 decibels at every setting, and this record cannot see a constant: what a take carries is the whole chain, and the run's bypass control says that chain is not transparent when its gains are centred. Separating them needs a chain whose unity gain is established rather than assumed, which is a calibration and not a sweep.

alternatives.reading: The grid is 1/127 because the reading is, and not because the unit is. Something in the capture or the analysis could quantise a level to one part in 127.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: Nothing in the chain has 127 in it. The take is 24-bit at 48 kHz, the level is a sum of squares over eight seconds published to two decimal places in decibels, and neither has a quantum near one part in a hundred and twenty-seven of amplitude. If the reading imposed the grid it would impose it on every sweep, and the frequency sweeps of the same session return levels that sit a fifth of a step from it.

alternatives.reading: The curve is a law after all, and the catalogue is missing it.

separated_by.observable: Whether the same address on another type returns the same hundred and twenty-eight multipliers.
separated_by.what_the_run_returned: It was run. Eleven settings over 26.5 dB on 01 40 agree with 01 00 to a worst 0.04 dB. That refutes a curve computed per type and it separates a table from a law by nothing at all, because both predicted exactly this.
separated_by.why_not_separable: A law that returns these hundred and twenty-eight numbers and a table holding them differ in where the numbers come from and in nothing that comes out, so no reading of this unit's output can tell them apart. The class does not rest on the difference: what is claimed is the multiplier and its quantum, and both readings give the same multiplier. What argues for the table is the era and not a measurement -- 128 entries cost 128 bytes -- and a prior may carry a claim and may not close one, so this stays open and says why.

alternatives.reading: The curve is what a type carries whose output is proportional to its input. Both types it has been read on are that: four filter sections, and a modulator with a delay line. A stage that saturates has a reason to scale its own output that neither of those has, and the byte is printed as that stage's output level.

separated_by.observable: Whether the same address on a type with a drive stage returns the same hundred and twenty-eight multipliers, and whether what it returns moves when the drive does.

predicts.the stored table, applied after the stag: The multipliers the two linear types returned, and the same curve at both drives. A gain applied after a stage cannot know how hard the stage was being driven.
predicts.a scaling the drive stage does itself: A curve that leaves the linear types' somewhere, and leaves itself between the two drives -- a level folded into a saturating stage is a level whose effect depends on what is arriving at it.

separated_by.sensitivity_here: 0.166 dB, the spread of one setting's own repeats on the second type. What has to clear it is one entry of the table, and how large that is depends on where in the byte it is read: 0.07 dB at the top of the range, 0.27 at setting 32 and 1.16 at setting 8. So the settings are weighted to the bottom, and the figure the margin is taken at is the coarsest of them that is still a reading.

run.why_this_type: It is the only family on this unit with a nonlinearity, and it is also the loudest thing the class can be read through -- which decides how far down the byte the reading reaches, because the stored curve and every law in the catalogue part company at the bottom and a setting is admitted only where it stands over the same chain's floor. The first type read reached setting 3 and the second only 8. Which type is loudest was measured rather than assumed: every candidate went through one short take of its own, and this one came back 5.7 dB over the first type at drive 0 and 2.9 at drive 96, against the second type by 12.0 and 9.2, and against the delay that looked like the obvious third type by 7.6 and 4.8 -- that delay being 1.9 dB quieter than the first type and so the worst of the candidates for this reading. Those are differences between types in one reading and not levels over the admission rule's floor, which is a different reading and a different number; what transfers between the two is the ordering and not the size. It also prints no balance, so nothing of the signal goes past the row being read.
run.why_two_drives: A curve measured once is a curve, and nothing in it says where in the chain it was applied. Two drives of the one stage that makes this type different say whether the byte is applied after that stage or inside it, which is the half of the question a third type alone cannot reach.

alternatives.ruled_out_by: The run it asked for was made, twice over, and the curve did not move. At the settings both drives admit the two agree to a worst 0.05 dB where one of these readings resolves 0.166, and each agrees with the first type to a worst 0.04 and 0.04 dB. A level the drive stage applied itself would have to move when the drive does; this one does not move at all, so the byte is applied after the stage and what it holds is the class's curve and not the stage's.

refuted_by: A setting whose multiplier sits a third of a step or more from the 1/127 grid while its take is well clear of the chain's silence, which no admitted setting does -- the worst is 0.24 of a step at setting 122, where one step is 0.068 decibels and the run resolves 0.01. Or another denominator scanned over the same settings coming closer, which none of the sixty-one does by a factor of ten. Or a level byte on another type returning multipliers that sit on no grid at all, which would make this a property of one effect rather than of how a gain is stored.

compared_against.why_not_a_filter: The set is one record and it was chosen rather than generated: the only sweep of this address that asked every one of the hundred and twenty-eight settings. That is a property of how a record was taken and not of where it is filed, so no filter over the index picks it out -- the same address on this type has another record that moved the byte at six settings while reading a corner, and it is not a reading of this class. The second type's sweep is held against this one record to record, which is stated under a_second_type rather than folded in here, because two measurements compared to each other with no model between them are not a model's comparison set.

settings.40 03 16: 125 of the 128 settings, all but 0, 1 and 2

stimulus: A held note through the effect, read as the level of the whole take against the run's own repeats of one setting.
domain.outside: The absolute gain, which the bypass control says this chain cannot give. Every type except 01 00. Setting 0, which is the effect off rather than a quiet setting of it. What the byte does to anything but the level -- a multiplier that changed the shape as well would not show in a figure that is one number per take.

residual.unit: decibels between the level a candidate law says and the level read
residual.why: the signed median swings 3.529 dB across the settings and 0 dB across the readings within one, against the run's own floor of 0.1357 dB

gross.why: The median residual over the span the effect commands, taken as the worst of the records scored. A rejection bound and not a target: below it the residual is reported and never optimised, because no candidate is decided by it.

qualitative.why: Properties the unit's readings have that the model's readings must have too. No arithmetic over a residual rescues a model that cuts where the unit boosts.

power.why: The runner-up in the catalogue, scored on the same records, and whether it leans or contradicts a property where the winner does neither. The decoy is not chosen -- it is whichever candidate came second, so a strawman cannot be put up in its place. A class holding one candidate is a catalogue that is unfinished, which is a finding and not a pass.

breakdown.why: A point worse than 0.5 of the span is a failure at that point rather than error at it. A residual that leans with the setting or with frequency is pointing at a structure the model does not have; one that does not is pointing at the room and the converters, and is not made smaller by anything this project can do.

reproduces.read_as: This block is the law race and not the claim. What it says is that the best formula in the catalogue breaks down: the byte read straight as the multiplier passes the gross gate at a twenty-second of the span and then leans, because it is out by three and a half decibels at the bottom of the byte and by a third of one at the top. The candidate that is the readout is not in this race -- its entries are the measurement, so a ranking that included it would rank the measurement first and call that a finding.

what_this_does_not_close.why: Four laws were held against it and the best is out by a median 1.61 decibels. The entries are published as a readout, which is what a hundred and twenty-eight free bytes look like from outside and is all anything downstream needs, but it is not a law and is not offered as one.
what_this_does_not_close.what_would: Nothing this project can measure. Once the table is free the values are a decision somebody made at a desk, and no sweep of the unit recovers the reasoning behind them. What a sweep can still do is say whether the same table is behind every type's level byte, which is the third alternative above and is queued.

what_this_does_not_close.what: Whether the byte is over 127 or over 128.
what_this_does_not_close.why: They differ by a constant 0.068 decibels and the chain's own insertion loss is four tenths of one, unmeasured. Recorded as equivalent rather than left open.
what_this_does_not_close.what_would: A chain whose unity gain is established -- the same stimulus recorded with the effect block switched out at the mixer rather than bypassed inside it. That is a calibration of the rig and not a sweep of the unit, and it would settle the same question for every level byte at once.

what_this_does_not_close.what: The other sixty-two types' level bytes.
what_this_does_not_close.why: All sixty-five are printed 0 - 127 against the last parameter of their list and none but this one has been swept. A table is pointed at, so the same printed range need not be the same table.
what_this_does_not_close.what_would: One sweep of a third type's level byte, on a type with a stage that saturates, which is the alternative this claim now carries.

what_this_does_not_close.what: The lowest setting. 0 sits 1.1 dB over the same chain's silence on every record that has asked it, which is not a reading of anything.
what_this_does_not_close.bounded_by: Its entry is the straight line's 0 and the table names it as not read. What would read it is a chain louder than any this class has been measured through, and the byte's own neighbours bound it: settings 1 and 2 both return a multiplier of 1, so whatever 0 returns is at most that and is either silence or one step of the grid.

what_this_does_not_close.what: Where between the stage and the output the byte sits. After the saturating stage is measured; whether it is before or after the two tone gains and the pan of the same trailing block is not.
what_this_does_not_close.bounded_by: Those three were held at the centre of their own ranges through every reading in this class, so nothing in these records depends on the order. What would separate it is the same sweep with one of them away from its centre, which is a run this claim does not need and does not queue.

what_it_would_change.what: Anything rendering an SC-series insertion effect at a level other than 127.
what_it_would_change.how: A renderer using the byte as the multiplier is three and a half decibels loud at the bottom of the byte and a decibel and a half loud through the middle of it, in the direction that matters: it is loud where a part was meant to sit back. The table is a hundred and twenty-eight bytes and removes all of it.

a_note_on_what_was_left_out: The candidate whose entries are the measurement was written, scored and then taken out of the ranking, and the first run of this class left it in -- where it came first with a residual of two ten-thousandths of the span and the four gates returned `reproduces`. That verdict was the measurement agreeing with itself. It is the same failure the equaliser's centre frequencies already had in this archive, where a model carrying twelve measured settings and interpolating between them was published as a law, and it is worth naming twice because it does not look like a failure from inside: every gate passes, the residual is beautiful, and nothing in the numbers says the model was copied from the thing it is being held against. What separates a readout from a law is whether it could have come out wrong, and a table with a free entry per setting could not. So the readout is published as a readout, its residual is reported as the reading's own rounding error, and the claim rests on the one thing a free table cannot arrange -- that the unrounded measurements sit on a grid, scanned against every nearby denominator.

a_second_type.what_was_asked: The same address, 40 03 16, on 01 40 -- a type with a modulator where the class was read on a type with none. Two measurements held against each other, with no model between them, which is the only comparison that can say whether the curve is one curve.
a_second_type.admitted_by: The class's own rule: a setting more than 20 dB over the silence taken through the same chain. Four fall under it here, at the bottom of the byte, where the type's own output sits nearer the floor than the other type's did.
a_second_type.what_it_settles: The curve is the machine's and not the type's. Over 11 settings and 26.5 dB of range the two types return the same gain to a median 0.01 dB and a worst 0.04, which is a fifth of what one of these readings resolves. Any reading in which a type carries its own gain curve is out by more than the measurement at every setting, and there is nothing left of it.
a_second_type.what_it_does_not_settle: Whether the numbers are stored or computed. A law that returns them and a table holding them both return them on every type, so agreement here was predicted by both readings and separates neither. That is written into the alternative rather than left as a gap.
a_second_type.why_that_matters: Every law in the catalogue was rejected on the first type and every one is rejected again here, on a different type, at settings chosen for where they differ. The nearest of them, the-byte-is-the-multiplier, is out by a median 1.999 dB against a floor of 0.136 and it leans. A second record is not a second opinion about the same takes -- it is the rejection holding where it had no reason to unless it is right.

a_third_type.what_was_asked: The same address, 40 03 16, on 01 11 -- the first type this class has been read on with a stage whose output is not proportional to its input -- and asked twice, at two drives of that stage. Two types had already settled that the curve is not computed per type. What they could not settle is where in the chain it is applied, because neither of them has anything that a gain applied before it and a gain applied after it would differ on.
a_third_type.what_it_settles: The byte is applied after the stage, and the curve is the class's. The two drives put the same multiplier at every setting both admit -- median 0.02 dB and worst 0.05 over 13 settings, against a floor of 0.166 -- and a gain folded into a saturating stage could not do that, because what it did would depend on what was arriving. Against the first type the worst disagreement is 0.04 dB at drive 0 and 0.04 dB at drive 96. So a third type agrees with the two linear ones, and it agrees through a stage of a kind neither of them has.
a_third_type.what_it_does_not_settle: Whether the numbers are stored or computed, which no reading of this unit's output can reach and which this claim already says so under its own alternative.
a_third_type.why_that_matters: The entries were read off the first type's sweep, so on that record they are the measurement agreeing with itself and are kept out of the ranking. Here they were fitted to nothing: two sweeps, a type they have never seen, and a stage of a kind no reading behind them had. A readout that survives that is a prediction, and it is the second time it has been one. The two settings whose entries this record itself supplied are left out of every score above, the rivals' as well as the readout's, so that what is compared is the same set of readings for all of them.
